title: Three-Week IB Economics Revision Plan for November
summary: IB Economics revision plan for November: prioritise weak topics, sharpen exam skills, practise timed papers, and protect rest across three focused weeks.
body_markdown:
This **IB Economics revision plan** gives November-session students a structure for their final 21 days: diagnose and repair knowledge in week one, practise exam answers in week two, then rehearse under timed conditions and protect recovery in week three.


Three weeks before an exam, every unfinished chapter can feel equally urgent. Some topics need rebuilding; others need a reminder. The useful question is where your next hour will make the greatest difference.


Start 21 days before your first Economics paper. Check your personal timetable before assigning sessions, especially when several subjects fall close together.


### The three-week plan at a glance


Week Main priority Economics workload Evidence of progress


Week one Diagnose and repair 45-60 minutes on most days Weaknesses become more specific


Week two Apply and evaluate 60-75 minutes on focused days Answers become clearer and more accurate


Week three Rehearse and recover Timed papers plus light review Timing improves and repeated errors decline


Prioritise weaknesses by likely mark return, alternate review with application, and reduce the workload when other subjects become urgent. Protect sleep throughout.


For supporting techniques, read[IB Economics revision methods that actually work](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/methods-for-effective-ib-economics-revision) .


### Week one: diagnose before you revise


### Build a traffic-light topic map


Organise your audit around microeconomics, macroeconomics, and the global economy, including development. HL students should flag calculations and policy analysis relevant to Paper 3.


Mark each subtopic:


- **Red:** you cannot explain the model, draw its diagram, or apply it confidently.
- **Amber:** you understand the theory but struggle with evaluation, examples, calculations, or unfamiliar contexts.
- **Green:** you can answer an exam-style question without substantial help.


Keep the map simple. A weakness connecting several question types, such as market failure or macroeconomic policy, usually deserves attention before an isolated definition.


Use the[IB Economics resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-economics) for Study Notes and Flashcards. Follow each short review with two or three relevant questions from the[IB Economics Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-economics/questionbank) .


### Give each session a clear purpose


A 60-minute session might include 15 minutes reviewing theory, 10 drawing diagrams from memory, 25 answering a focused question, and 10 checking mistakes.


Separate errors into knowledge, application, evaluation, diagrams, calculations, and timing. “Revise macroeconomics” offers little direction. “Explain why this event shifts aggregate supply” gives tomorrow's session a target.


For diagrams, practise the explanation alongside the drawing. Label both axes, identify the initial equilibrium, show the relevant change, and explain the resulting effects. Then check whether your written argument actually refers to those changes. A familiar picture offers limited help if the reasoning beside it remains vague or incomplete.


Finish the week with a short mixed-topic test. Use the results to update your priorities before adding more revision hours.


### Week two: turn knowledge into marks


Knowing a theory and writing a convincing answer require different practice. Paper 1 uses extended response; Paper 2 uses data response. HL students also complete the policy-focused Paper 3. Review[Paper 1 versus Paper 2 explained](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-economics-paper-1-vs-paper-2) if your preparation treats every question alike.


### Rotate the skills your answers need


Across the week, practise four skills:


- **Explanation:** define terms and build clear chains of reasoning.
- **Application:** connect theory to the stimulus or real-world context.
- **Evaluation:** weigh assumptions, stakeholders, time periods, and policy trade-offs.
- **Quantitative work:** select formulas, show working, and interpret results.


Attempt an answer without notes, review it, then rewrite its weakest paragraph. This isolates the problem without spending an entire session copying improved material. Use the[IB Economics exam tips guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-economics-exam-tips) to sharpen command terms, diagrams, and evaluation.


Make evaluation specific to the question. For a proposed subsidy, consider who benefits, how producers might respond, the opportunity cost of government spending, and whether the policy addresses the underlying problem. Finish with a judgement that explains which condition matters most. Listing advantages and disadvantages alone leaves that judgement unfinished.


Move from topic questions towards mixed sets. Ask RevisionDojo's AI Chat to unpack difficult reasoning, and use grading tools to identify missing development. Check uncertain feedback against teacher guidance.


A student asks a calendar to fit in another topic while the calendar insists on preserving a nap.


### Keep examples compact and accurate


Build a small example bank covering taxation, subsidies, inflation, unemployment, trade, exchange rates, and development strategies. Record the place, policy, approximate period, relevant theory, and one limitation. Verify details rather than memorising uncertain statistics.


For extended responses,[How to get a 7 in IB Economics](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-get-a-7-in-ib-economics) provides further guidance on developing analysis.


### Week three: rehearse, correct, and taper


Rehearse each paper format you will sit, using timed sections when full papers would overwhelm your schedule. Paper 1 lasts 1 hour 15 minutes; Paper 2 and HL Paper 3 each last 1 hour 45 minutes. Confirm arrangements against your examination timetable.


RevisionDojo's Predicted Papers and Mock Exams can provide unfamiliar practice. Remove notes, follow the time limit, and continue after imperfect answers. Rehearsal exposes pacing problems that isolated questions can hide.


Before starting, divide the available time between reading, planning, answering, and checking. Use the marks available to guide how much attention each part receives. If one section overruns, record why during your review. You can then practise a shorter plan or a more direct explanation in your next timed session.


### Make review part of every attempt


After each timed attempt:


- identify where you gained or lost time;
- compare your reasoning with available mark guidance;
- select the three errors most likely to recur;
- redo affected questions two days later;
- add missing definitions, diagrams, or formulas to Flashcards.


Correct the problem before sitting another full paper. Consult[IB Economics last-minute revision priorities](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-economics-last-minute-revision-priorities) when deciding what still deserves attention.


During the final 48 hours, review your error log, essential diagrams, formulas, command terms, and examples. Keep retrieval short. Confirm equipment, travel, and start times, then finish early enough to sleep properly.


### Fit Economics around your other subjects


On crowded days, use a 25-minute session: retrieve five definitions, draw two diagrams, and outline one evaluative paragraph. Reserve longer blocks for timed practice. Reduce passive rereading first when the calendar becomes overloaded.


RevisionDojo brings Questionbank practice, Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, grading tools, Predicted Papers, and Mock Exams into one workflow. Its Coursework Library and Tutors provide broader support, while your final weeks should centre on the errors your practice reveals. Begin with one red topic and one question today, then let the result guide tomorrow's work.
